extracted.intended_audience: poets, painters, orators, and other artists/critics seeking to move the passions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for artists and writers on producing effects of the sublime and beautiful by understanding human passions (sympathy, imitation, ambition, terror, obscurity, power) and applying techniques (obscurity, realism, imitation vs. nature) to move audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and classify the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: The passions are usefully divided with regard to their final cause: those belonging to self-preservation (turning on pain and danger) and those belonging to society (love, sympathy, imitation, ambition); each has distinct operations and effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To affect the passions deliberately you must 'know the exact boundaries of their several jurisdictions' and 'pursue them through all their variety of operations'; theoretical knowledge of these classes helps artists affect them 'after a delicate manner' and judge works designed to affect them.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sublime produces astonishment (suspension of faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The passion caused by the great and sublime in nature is astonishment: 'that state of the soul in which all its motions are suspended, with some degree of horror.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to overwhelm the audience's reasoning and ordinary mental motions so the mind is entirely filled with the object; lesser effects are admiration, reverence, and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terror is central to the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: No passion so effectually robs the mind of all its powers of acting and reasoning as fear; 'whatever therefore is terrible ... is sublime too' regardless of size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create sublimity, introduce an apprehension of pain or death (or ideas that connote danger). Even small objects can be sublime if they provoke terror (e.g., serpents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity heightens terror and sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: To make anything very terrible, obscurity seems in general to be necessary; when we know the full extent of danger, apprehension vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uncertainty, darkness, or ambiguous description (night, shadow, indistinctness) to augment dread and the sublime. Examples: temple darkness, Milton's description of Death—'all is dark, uncertain, confused, terrible, and sublime to the last degree.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness often reduces affect; obscurity can increase emotional power
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one thing to make an idea clear, and another to make it affecting; a clear idea is 'another name for a little idea.' Obscure, confused images can produce stronger emotions than very clear ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer verbal, suggestive, or crowded/confused imagery (poetry, rhetoric) when you wish to move passions strongly rather than precise, distinct pictorial detail; use obscurity intentionally rather than accidental vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism strengthens imitative arts' power
rubrics_metrics.description: The nearer a representation approaches the reality, and the further it removes us from all idea of fiction, the more perfect is its power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In tragedy and imitative arts strive for representations that approach reality to maximize emotional effect; yet remember that real events will always surpass imitation in power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish imitation-based power from sympathy-based power
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule: 'When the object represented in poetry or painting is such as we could have no desire of seeing in the reality, then I may be sure that its power in poetry or painting is owing to the power of imitation.' Otherwise the effect is more due to the nature of the thing (sympathy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose whether your audience's response comes from admiring the skill of imitation (still-life, exact copying) or from being moved by the object's own affective character; design accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit sympathy to transfer feelings to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy 'puts us in the place of another man, and affects us in many respects as he is affected' — it is how poetry and the arts transfuse passions from one breast to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters' states palpable so readers or viewers take on those states; note that sympathy can make suffering a source of complex pleasure (delight blended with uneasiness), which artists can harness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is a primary mode of learning and pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: It is by imitation far more than by precept that we learn everything; imitation produces pleasure and forms manners, opinions, and lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imitation (mimicry, representation) as a pedagogic and pleasurable device, but be aware it can lead to mechanical copying if unchecked by other principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition drives improvement; avoid mere slavish imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: If men gave themselves up to imitation entirely there could be no improvement; God has planted ambition and the pleasure of excelling, which drives men to distinguish themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage originality and the aspiration to 'excel' in your practice; balance imitation (useful as foundation) with ambition to innovate and improve artistic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representations of vast power should connote danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing sublime that is not some modification of power; the idea of vast power is connected to ideas of pain, violence, and terror, and so becomes sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying strength or greatness, emphasize its potential for harm or dominance (or preserve latent menace) to preserve sublimity; stripping strength of danger makes it contemptible rather than grand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's obscurity can outdo painting for eliciting grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry raises obscure and confused ideas that can hurry the mind out of itself; painting presents clearer ideas and, after allowing for imitation, seldom rouses passions as powerfully as poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor verbal strategies that assemble large, confused images (crowds of great images) for grandeur; painting may need judicious obscurity to approach similar effects, but beware of making grotesque literalizations of poetic chimeras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground artistic rules in nature and psychology rather than mere precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics who seek rules for the arts among other artworks err; 'the true standard of the arts is in every man's power' and 'an easy observation of the most common...things in nature' gives the truest light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base craft on observation of human nature and the causes of passions rather than slavish imitation of earlier artists; theoretical understanding clears the way for better practice and criticism.
